title: Urinary Catheterization
keywords: blood at the urethral meatus, a high-riding or non-palpable prostate, or perineal/scrotal hematoma after pelvic trauma means stop and get imaging before a urethral catheter
coude tip catheter for a male with suspected BPH when a standard catheter won't pass
do not force a catheter against resistance
CAUTI is a real and largely preventable complication, use only when genuinely indicated and remove promptly
sources: Standard emergency medicine/nursing procedural references for urethral and suprapubic catheterization.
CDC guidance on catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI) prevention.

changelog.change: Initial entry — a genuine content gap (Content audit 2026-09-14, Batch 5).

purpose: Urethral catheterization technique, the trauma-related red flags that mean stop and image before catheterizing, and the CAUTI-prevention principle of using a catheter only when genuinely indicated.
entryPrompt: In a trauma patient, screen for urethral injury red flags BEFORE attempting urethral catheterization — proceeding despite them can convert a partial urethral injury into a complete one.

nodes.prompt: Trauma patients — screen for urethral injury first
nodes.body: STOP and do NOT attempt urethral catheterization — get urologic imaging/consultation first — if ANY of these are present after pelvic/perineal trauma: blood at the urethral meatus, a high-riding or non-palpable prostate on rectal exam, or a perineal/scrotal/labial hematoma. Any of these suggests a urethral injury, and passing a catheter blindly risks converting a partial tear into a complete transection, or creating a false passage. If a urethral injury is suspected, a retrograde urethrogram (or urology-directed alternative) should precede any catheterization attempt.

Sterile technique: prep the periurethral area, use sterile lubricant (with lidocaine gel if available/tolerated, instilled into the urethra before insertion for a male — this meaningfully reduces discomfort and is underused). Insert the catheter gently and steadily; a normal male urethra has a natural resistance at the external sphincter — steady gentle pressure (not force) with reassurance and having the patient relax/take a breath usually overcomes it. Advance to the hub before inflating the balloon (inflating in the urethra rather than the bladder is a real, avoidable injury) — confirm urine return first.

nodes.prompt: 2. If you meet resistance — do not force it
nodes.body: Do NOT force a catheter against significant resistance — this risks creating a false passage or worsening an unrecognized stricture/injury. For a male with known or suspected BPH where a standard catheter won't pass, a COUDE-TIP catheter (curved tip, inserted with the tip pointing anteriorly/upward) is designed to navigate around an enlarged prostate more easily. If a coude catheter and gentle technique still fail, stop and involve urology rather than escalating force or repeated attempts.

nodes.prompt: 3. When urethral catheterization isn't possible or appropriate
nodes.body: Suprapubic catheterization (a separate procedure, generally urology-performed or under urology guidance in most EDs unless a specific credentialed provider and kit are available) is the alternative when urethral catheterization is contraindicated (suspected urethral injury) or has failed despite reasonable attempts, in a patient with a genuine indication for bladder drainage (urinary retention, monitoring).

nodes.prompt: CAUTI prevention — use only when genuinely indicated, remove promptly
nodes.body: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection is a common, largely preventable hospital-acquired complication. Place a urinary catheter only for a genuine indication (urinary retention, accurate output monitoring in a critically ill patient, specific surgical/wound-healing needs, patient immobility with a stage 3-4 pressure injury where urine contact would worsen it) — NOT routinely 'for convenience' or because a patient is incontinent without another specific indication. Document the indication, and reassess daily whether the catheter is still needed — prompt removal once the indication resolves is one of the most effective, evidence-supported CAUTI-prevention measures available.

checklist: Trauma red flags (blood at meatus, high-riding/non-palpable prostate, perineal/scrotal hematoma) screened for before attempting urethral catheterization in a trauma patient
Balloon inflated only after confirmed urine return and full hub insertion, not in the urethra
No forcing against resistance — coude catheter or urology involvement for a difficult male catheterization
A genuine indication documented, with a plan to remove the catheter promptly once it's no longer needed
buildNote: workflow outputType. The trauma-red-flags warning node is placed first and deliberately framed as an absolute stop, since this is the single highest-stakes decision point in this otherwise routine procedure.
